评测方法：CircularEval 将一道含 N 个选项的问题循环移位为 N 种顺序；模型须在所有轮次都答对，该题才计为正确。自由文本回答无法直接提取选项时，使用 GPT-4 匹配对应选项，以减少严格字符串匹配造成的误判。
2024 年 评估对真实物理环境的空间理解能力，涵盖物体相对位置、距离判断、方向识别、物体大小比较及道路场景理解等。数据包含车辆拍摄的匿名化图像及其他真实场景图像。 图像：0.8K
问题：0.8K		 Accuracy

评测维度中文名称评测内容
一、空间理解（Spatial Understanding）：9 个
1. Scene Understanding场景理解理解图像整体场景和语义
2. Instance Identity物体识别识别物体类别或判断其是否存在

10. Action Recognition动作识别识别视频中的具体动作
11. Action Prediction动作预测根据已有视频预测后续动作

Li et al. SEED-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs with Generative Comprehension. arXiv:2307.16125, 2023. 论文链接 · 官方仓库。

注：规模采用原论文 Table 1 的 19,242 道选择题，包含 9 个图像空间理解维度与 3 个视频时序理解维度。原论文采用候选答案似然排序确定预测选项，并以 Accuracy 评估。
2022 年 面向小学至高中科学教育的多模态问答基准，采用多项选择题，覆盖自然科学、社会科学和语言科学，还提供背景知识和答案解释。 图像：7.8K
问题：21.2K		 Accuracy
Lu et al. Learn to Explain: Multimodal Reasoning via Thought Chains for Science Question Answering. NeurIPS, 2022. arXiv:2209.09513. 论文链接。

数据集构成：共 21,208 道题目，涵盖 3 个学科、26 个主题（Topics）、127 个类别（Categories）、379 项具体技能（Skills）及 1–12 年级。Train / Val / Test 分别为 12,726 / 4,241 / 4,241 道。

上下文：10,332 道（48.7%）包含图像，10,220 道（48.2%）包含文本；其中 6,532 道（30.8%）同时包含图像和文本，7,188 道（33.9%）不含额外上下文。图像包括自然图像与科学示意图。

标注与评测：17,798 道（83.9%）提供 Lecture，19,202 道（90.5%）提供 Explanation。主指标为 Accuracy；解释生成质量还可用 BLEU、ROUGE-L、Sentence-BERT Similarity 及人工评估（相关性、正确性、完整性）衡量。
2024 年 从现有多模态基准收集候选样本，减少无需图像即可作答的问题及训练数据泄漏。包含。 样本：1.5K Accuracy

实例推理Instance Reasoning (IR)Single-instance Attribute Reasoning（单实例属性推理）、Cross-instance Attribute Comparison（跨实例属性比较）、Cross-instance Relation Reasoning（跨实例关系推理）
逻辑推理Logical Reasoning (LR)Diagram Reasoning（图表推理）、Code & Sequence Reasoning（代码与序列推理）、Common Reasoning（常识推理）

Chen et al. Are We on the Right Way for Evaluating Large Vision-Language Models? arXiv:2403.20330, 2024. 论文链接。

数据构建：从 MMBench、SEED-Bench、MMMU、ScienceQA、AI2D 和 MathVista 收集 22,401 条候选样本，经 8 个 LLM 检查器过滤后保留 11,607 条，再结合 16 个 LVLM 的答题表现划分难度，并由 3 位专家审核，最终选出 1,500 条样本。六大核心能力各含 250 条，并尽可能均衡覆盖 18 个细分维度。构建原则包括视觉依赖性、最小化数据泄漏和高级多模态能力。

评测指标：Accuracy 用于衡量整体及各维度表现。辅助指标包括 Multi-modal Gain（MG = Sᵥ − S₍wv₎，衡量有图像与无图像输入的准确率差异）和 Multi-modal Leakage（ML = max(0, S₍wv₎ − Sₜ)，估计多模态训练可能引入的数据泄漏；Sₜ 为对应原始语言模型准确率）。

评测设置：纯 LLM 使用 2-shot，LVLM 使用 0-shot。论文实验中，纯 LLM 平均准确率为 24.6%，GPT-4V（High）最高为 57.1%；MMStar 平均 ML 为 1.9。

Mishra et al. OCR-VQA: Visual Question Answering by Reading Text in Images. ICDAR, 2019. 论文链接 · 数据集主页。

数据集构成：OCR-VQA-200K 包含 207,572 张书籍封面图像和 1,002,146 个问答对，平均每张图像对应 4.83 个问题；包含 117,378 位作者、203,471 个书名、32 种图书类别和 320,794 个不同答案。Train / Val / Test 按 80% / 10% / 10% 划分，测试集约 100K 个问答对。

问题类型：Book Title（书名）、Author Name（作者）、Book Genre（类别）、Year（出版年份）和 Edition（版本）。书名、作者和类别是主要任务；年份与版本仅在部分封面中出现。问题基于模板生成，并经人工改写以增加表达多样性。

评测指标：Accuracy，即预测正确的问题占比。论文报告的最佳基线模型 BLOCK+CNN+W2V 整体准确率为 48.3%；二分类问题为 58.2%，书籍类别识别为 22.0%，作者识别为 42.9%。
2023 年 综合 OCR 评测基准，涵盖 5 大任务：文字识别、场景文字问答、文档问答、关键信息抽取和手写数学公式识别。 样本：1.0K Score（满分 1,000）
Liu et al. OCRBench: On the Hidden Mystery of OCR in Large Multimodal Models. arXiv:2305.07895, 2023. 论文链接 · 官方仓库。

数据集构成：共 1,000 个经人工筛选和校正的问答样本：文字识别 300 个、场景文字问答 200 个、文档问答 200 个、关键信息抽取 200 个、手写数学公式识别 100 个。文字识别覆盖常规、不规则、艺术字、手写、数字串和非语义文本；非语义文本通过打乱单词中字母顺序构造，以检验模型是否真正识别字符。

评测指标：采用统一的 GT-in-output 判定，模型回答包含 Ground Truth 即算正确；五大任务的正确样本数相加得到 Score，满分 1,000。考虑到模型回答常包含解释，论文未直接沿用原始任务的 Exact Match 或 ANLS；同时过滤短答案样本，并人工核验、修正答案及补充多答案。关键信息抽取任务还使用专门提示词，要求模型直接依据图中文字回答。

评测特点：重点考察非语义字符、模糊图像、多语言文字、手写文本及数学公式。论文报告多模态大模型在非语义文本上的平均表现较语义文本下降 57.0%，传统场景文字识别 SOTA 方法约下降 4.6%；模型在手写文本、中文识别和手写数学公式方面仍有不足，文档问答和关键信息抽取也对图像分辨率要求较高。

数据规模：测试集 5,188 个问题、1,287 张图像；完整数据集 50,000 个问题、12,767 张图像。数据划分：Train / Val / Test = 80% / 10% / 10%。

ANLS（Average Normalized Levenshtein Similarity）：基于编辑距离计算预测答案与标准答案的相似度，降低 OCR 拼写错误等细微差异带来的惩罚。

Accuracy：预测答案与任意一个 Ground Truth 完全匹配的比例。

问题：2.5K		 Relaxed Accuracy

Example 1

Question: what color was john wilkes booth’s hair

Wikipedia Page: John_Wilkes_Booth

Long answer: Some critics called Booth “the handsomest man in America” and a “natural genius”, and noted his having an “astonishing memory”; others were mixed in their estimation of his acting. He stood 5 feet 8 inches (1.73 m) tall, had jet-black hair, and was lean and athletic. Noted Civil War reporter George Alfred Townsend described him as a “muscular, perfect man” with “curling hair, like a Corinthian capital”.

Short answer: jet-black

Example 2

Question: can you make and receive calls in airplane mode

Wikipedia Page: Airplane_mode

Long answer: Airplane mode, aeroplane mode, flight mode, offline mode, or standalone mode is a setting available on many smartphones, portable computers, and other electronic devices that, when activated, suspends radio-frequency signal transmission by the device, thereby disabling Bluetooth, telephony, and Wi-Fi. GPS may or may not be disabled, because it does not involve transmitting radio waves.

Short answer: BOOLEAN:NO

Example 3

Question: why does queen elizabeth sign her name elizabeth r

Wikipedia Page: Royal-sign-manual

Long answer: The royal sign-manual usually consists of the sovereign’s regnal name (without number, if otherwise used), followed by the letter R for Rex (King) or Regina (Queen). Thus, the signs-manual of both Elizabeth I and Elizabeth II read Elizabeth R. When the British monarch was also Emperor or Empress of India, the sign manual ended with R I, for Rex Imperator or Regina Imperatrix (King-Emperor/Queen-Empress).

Short answer: NULL

entry.title: On the Concentration of Empirical Means on the Simplex

link.title: On the Concentration of Empirical Means on the Simplex

entry.content:
Many statistical or machine learning problems start from the same basic question:

Given finitely many samples, how accurately can we estimate an expectation?

Let us begin with the simplest case.

1. Estimating the mean of a single random variable

Suppose \(X \in [0,1]\) is a scalar random variable with mean \(\mu=\mathbb{E}[X].\) Given \(N\) i.i.d. samples \(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(N)}\), the natural estimator is the sample mean \(\hat{\mu}=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N X^{(n)}.\)

A classic result, Hoeffding’s inequality, tells us that for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), the probability that the absolute difference between \(\mu\) and \(\hat{\mu}\) exceeds \(\varepsilon > 0\) is at most \(2\exp(-2N\varepsilon^2)\),

\[\mathbb{P}\left(|\hat{\mu}-\mu| \geq \varepsilon \right) \leq 2\exp(-2N\varepsilon^2)。\]

This captures the basic message of finite-sample mean estimation: as the number of samples grows, the empirical mean concentrates around the true mean, with deviation on the order of \(1/\sqrt{N}\).

So far, everything is completely standard. We are estimating one number, and Hoeffding gives a clean answer.

2. From a scalar to a vector

Now let us move from a scalar to a \(K\)-dimensional random vector \(X=(X_1,...,X_K) \in \mathbb{R}^K,\) and suppose we want to estimate its mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbb{E}[X].\) Given i.i.d. samples \(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(N)}\), we again use the empirical mean \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N X^{(n)}.\)

At first glance, the most natural strategy is coordinate-wise estimation. If each coordinate satisfies \(X_i \in [0,1]\), then Hoeffding applies coordinate by coordinate:

\[\mathbb{P}\left(|\hat{\mu}_i-\mu_i| \geq \varepsilon \right) \leq 2\exp(-2N\varepsilon^2)。\]

This is fine as far as it goes. But it only tells us that each coordinate is accurate separately. It does not yet say how well the whole vector is estimated. If we care about the entire vector, a natural quantity is \(\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^K|\hat{\mu}_i-\mu_i|.\)

One can still start from coordinate-wise Hoeffding and then combine the results using a union bound.

Theorem 1 Hoeffding's inequality for vector samples

For any \(\varepsilon > 0\), the probability that the \(L_1\) distance between \({\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\) exceeds \(\varepsilon\) is at most \(2K\exp(-\frac{2N\epsilon^2}{K^2})\):

\[\mathbb{P}\left(\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\|_1 \geq \varepsilon \right) \leq 2K\exp(-\frac{2N\varepsilon^2}{K^2}).\]
Proof (Click to expand)

If \(\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\|_1 \ge t,\) then at least one coordinate must satisfy \(|\hat{\mu}_i-\mu_i| \ge \frac{\varepsilon}{K},\) since otherwise all \(K\) coordinates would be smaller than \(\varepsilon/K\), and their sum could not reach \(\varepsilon\). Hence

\[\mathbb{P}\!\left(\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\|_1 \ge t\right) \le \sum_{i=1}^K \mathbb{P}\!\left(|\hat{\mu}_i-\mu_i| \ge \frac{\varepsilon}{K}\right) \le 2K\exp\!\left(-\frac{2N\varepsilon^2}{K^2}\right),\]

where the last step follows from Hoeffding’s inequality applied coordinate-wise.

□

But this approach is somewhat crude: it treats the vector simply as a collection of unrelated coordinates, without using any additional structure the vector might have. And in many problems, that structure matters.

3. A special case: simplex-valued random vectors

Now suppose that \(X=(X_1,...,X_K)\) is not arbitrary, but lies in the probability simplex (\(\Delta^{K-1}\)):

\[X_i \geq 0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^K X_i= 1.\]

This setting appears naturally when \(X\) represents a label distribution, a soft label, or a probabilistic prediction. In this case, the mean and the empirical mean also lie in the simplex

\[\mathbf{p}=\mathbb{E}[X] \in \Delta^{K-1}, \quad \hat{\mathbf{p}}=\frac1N \sum_{n=1}^N X^{(n)} \in \Delta^{K-1}.\]

This is the point where coordinate-wise Hoeffding begins to feel mismatched to the problem. It is still usable, but it does not fully reflect the fact that the object of interest is a distribution (simplex).

A concentration result for general simplex-valued samples can be obtained from McDiarmid’s inequality.

Theorem 2 Concentration inequality for general simplex-valued samples

For any \(t>0\),

\[\mathbb{P}\left( \|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \ge \sqrt{\frac{K}{N}}+t \right) \le \exp\left(-\frac{Nt^2}{2}\right).\]

Equivalently, for any \(\delta\in(0,1)\), with probability at least \(1-\delta\),

\[\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \le \sqrt{\frac{K}{N}} + \sqrt{\frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{N}}.\]
Proof (Click to expand)

Define

\[f\big(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(N)}\big) = \left\| \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N X^{(n)}-\mathbf{p} \right\|_1.\]

If we replace one sample \(X^{(j)}\) by another simplex point \(\tilde X^{(j)}\), then by the triangle inequality,

\[\left| f(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(j)},\dots,X^{(N)}) - f(X^{(1)},\dots,\tilde X^{(j)},\dots,X^{(N)}) \right| \le \frac{1}{N}\|X^{(j)}-\tilde X^{(j)}\|_1.\]

Now any two points in the simplex are at \(L_1\) distance at most 2, so \(\left|f(\cdots)-f(\cdots)\right|\le \frac{2}{N}.\)

Therefore, McDiarmid’s inequality gives

\[\mathbb{P}\left(f-\mathbb{E}f\ge t\right) \le \exp\left( -\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{n=1}^N (2/N)^2} \right) = \exp\left(-\frac{Nt^2}{2}\right),\]

which proves

\[\mathbb{P}\left( \|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \ge \mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1+t \right) \le \exp\left(-\frac{Nt^2}{2}\right).\]

It remains to bound the expectation term. By Cauchy–Schwarz, \(\|\mathbf{u}\|_1\le \sqrt{K}\,\|\mathbf{u}\|_2,\) hence

\[\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \le \sqrt{K}\,\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_2 \le \sqrt{K}\,\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_2^2}.\]

Since the samples are independent, \(\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_2^2 = \frac{1}{N}\,\mathbb{E}\|X-\mathbf{p}\|_2^2.\)

Also, because \(\mathbf{p}=\mathbb{E}[X]\), \(\mathbb{E}\|X-\mathbf{p}\|_2^2 = \mathbb{E}\|X\|_2^2-\|\mathbf{p}\|_2^2.\)

Finally, since \(X\in\Delta^{K-1}\), \(\|X\|_2^2 = \sum_{i=1}^K X_i^2 \le \left(\sum_{i=1}^K X_i\right)^2 = 1.\) Therefore, \(\mathbb{E}\|X-\mathbf{p}\|_2^2 \le \mathbb{E}\|X\|_2^2 \le 1.\)

Combining the above inequalities yields \(\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \le \sqrt{K}\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}} = \sqrt{\frac{K}{N}}.\)

Substituting this into the McDiarmid bound gives \(\mathbb{P}\left( \|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \ge \sqrt{\frac{K}{N}}+t \right) \le \exp\left(-\frac{Nt^2}{2}\right).\) Finally, setting \(t=\sqrt{\frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{N}}\) gives the high-probability form \(\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \le \sqrt{\frac{K}{N}} + \sqrt{\frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{N}}\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

□

3.1 The most extreme simplex case: one-hot samples

A particularly important special case is when each sample lies at a vertex of the simplex:

\[X \in \{\mathbf{e}_1,...,\mathbf{e}_K\},\]

where \(\mathbf{e}_i\) is the \(i\)-th standard basis vector. This means that each sample is a one-hot vector, or equivalently, a hard categorical label. In this setting, \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}=\frac1N \sum_{n=1}^N X^{(n)}\) is exactly the empirical class frequency, and \(\mathbf{p}=\mathbb{E}[X]\) is the true categorical distribution. It is precisely the classical problem of estimating a categorical distribution from finitely many samples. And for this problem, Weissman’s inequality directly controls the \(L_1\) error of the empirical distribution:

Theorem 3 Weissman's inequality for one-hot samples

If \(X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(N)}\) are i.i.d. one-hot samples from a categorical distribution \(\mathbf{p}\), then for any \(\varepsilon > 0\),

\[\mathbb{P}\left(\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \geq \varepsilon \right) \leq (2^K-2)\exp\left(-\frac{N\varepsilon^2}{2}\right)\]

3.3 Comparing the sample complexity

A convenient way to compare the bounds is to ask the following question:

How many samples do we need in order to guarantee \(\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \leq \varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\)?

Hoeffding’s inequality

The sample complexity is

\[N = \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K^2(\log K+\log(1/\delta))}{\varepsilon^2}\right).\]

So here the sample size scales quadratically in \(K\), up to logarithmic factors.

Proof (Click to expand)

We require

\[2K\exp(-\frac{2N\varepsilon^2}{K^2}) \leq \delta\]

Taking logarithms gives

\[N \geq \frac{K^2}{2\varepsilon^2}\left(\log(2K)+\log\frac1\delta\right)\]

Therefore, the resulting sample complexity is

\[N = \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K^2(\log K+\log(1/\delta))}{\varepsilon^2}\right).\]
□

Inequality for general simplex-valued samples

The sample complexity is

\[N = \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right).\]

So the required number of samples again grows linearly in \(K\).

Proof (Click to expand)

From the general simplex concentration bound, with probability at least \(1-\delta\),

\[\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \le \sqrt{\frac{K}{N}} + \sqrt{\frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{N}}.\]

Therefore, to ensure \(\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \le \varepsilon,\) it is enough to require \(\sqrt{\frac{K}{N}} + \sqrt{\frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{N}} \le \varepsilon.\)

Factoring out \(1/\sqrt{N}\) gives

\[\frac{\sqrt{K}+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)}}{\sqrt{N}} \le \varepsilon,\]

which is equivalent to

\[N \ge \frac{\left(\sqrt{K}+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)}\right)^2}{\varepsilon^2}.\]

Expanding the square,

\(N \ge \frac{K+2\log(1/\delta)+2\sqrt{2K\log(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon^2}.\) Thus, \(N = \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K+\log(1/\delta)+\sqrt{K\log(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon^2}\right).\)

In particular, this implies \(N = \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right).\)

□

Weissman’s inequality

The sample complexity is

\[N=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K+\log1/\delta}{\varepsilon^2}\right)\]

So the required number of samples grows linearly in \(K\).

Proof (Click to expand)

We require

\[(2^K-2)\exp\left(-\frac{N\varepsilon^2}{2}\right) \leq \delta\]

Taking logarithms gives

\[N \geq \frac{2}{\varepsilon^2}\left(\log(2^K-2)+\log \frac1\delta\right)\]

Since \(\log(2^K-2)\approx K\log 2\), this means that Weissman’s inequality yields the sample complexity

\[N=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K+\log\frac1\delta}{\varepsilon^2}\right)\]

So the required number of samples grows linearly in \(K\).

□

This comparison makes the difference transparent:

\(\text{General simplex: } \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K}{\varepsilon^2}\right),\) \(\text{Weissman (one-hot): } \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K}{\varepsilon^2}\right),\) \(\text{Hoeffding: } \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{K^2\log K}{\varepsilon^2}\right).\)

In other words, the coordinate-wise Hoeffding argument loses a full factor of \(K\) in dimension dependence because it reduces an \(L_1\) deviation event to \(K\) separate coordinate events. By contrast, both Weissman’s inequality and the general simplex bound achieve essentially linear dependence on \(K\).

3.3.1 Choice of norm matters

It is also worth noting that this gap is largely a consequence of measuring error in \(L_1\) distance. For \(L_1\), the coordinate-wise Hoeffding argument must first reduce the event \(\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1 \ge \varepsilon\) to the existence of at least one coordinate deviation of size \(\varepsilon/K\), which is exactly where the extra factor of \(K^2\) in the exponent comes from. By contrast, if we measure the error in \(L_\infty\) distance, then

\[\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_\infty \ge \varepsilon \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists i \in [K] \text{ such that } |\hat p_i-p_i|\ge \varepsilon.\]

In this case, a direct union bound together with coordinate-wise Hoeffding already gives

\[\mathbb{P}\left(\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}-\mathbf{p}\|_\infty \ge \varepsilon\right) \le \sum_{i=1}^K \mathbb{P}\left(|\hat p_i-p_i|\ge \varepsilon\right) \le 2K\exp(-2N\varepsilon^2).\]

So for \(L_\infty\), the coordinate-wise argument is already of the correct order, with only a logarithmic dependence on \(K\) in the corresponding sample complexity. In other words, the main advantage of Weissman’s inequality (or inequality for general simplex-valued samples) is not just that it is better in general, but that it is much better matched to the geometry of the \(L_1\) distance on distributions.

3.4 One-hot samples as a worst-case upper bound

To compare the general simplex samples (soft) with the categorical one-hot case, define a hardened sample

\[Y^{(n)} \in \{\mathbf{e}_1,\dots,\mathbf{e}_K\}\]

by drawing

\[\mathbb{P}\!\left(Y^{(n)}=\mathbf{e}_i \mid X^{(n)}\right)=X_i^{(n)}, \qquad i=1,\dots,K.\]

That is, conditional on the soft vector \(X^{(n)}\), we sample a one-hot vector according to its coordinates. By construction, \(\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y^{(n)} \mid X^{(n)}\right] = X^{(n)},\) and therefore \(\mathbb{E}[Y^{(n)}] = \mathbb{E}[X^{(n)}] = \mathbf{p}.\) So the hard and soft samples have the same mean, but the hard sample is more extreme since it lives on the vertices of the simplex. The key observation is that this hardening operation can only increase dispersion under convex losses.

Theorem 4

For any convex function \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^K \to \mathbb{R}\),

\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\varphi\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathsf{soft}}-\mathbf{p}\right)\right] \le \mathbb{E}\!\left[\varphi\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathsf{hard}}-\mathbf{p}\right)\right],\]

where \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathsf{hard}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N Y^{(n)}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathsf{soft}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N X^{(n)}.\)

Proof (Click to expand)

Since \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{hard}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N Y^{(n)},\) we have

\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{hard}} \mid X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(N)}\right] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \mathbb{E}\!\left[Y^{(n)} \mid X^{(n)}\right] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N X^{(n)} = \hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{soft}}.\]

Therefore, \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{soft}}-\mathbf{p} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{hard}}-\mathbf{p}\mid X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(N)}\right].\) Applying Jensen’s inequality conditionally gives

\[\varphi\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{soft}}-\mathbf{p}\right) = \varphi\!\left( \mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{hard}}-\mathbf{p}\mid X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(N)}\right] \right) \le \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \varphi\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{hard}}-\mathbf{p}\right) \middle| X^{(1)},\dots,X^{(N)} \right].\]

Taking expectation on both sides proves the claim.

□

In particular, taking \(\varphi(\mathbf{u})=\|\mathbf{u}\|_1\) shows that \(\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathsf{soft}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1\right] \le \mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathsf{hard}}-\mathbf{p}\|_1\right].\) Therefore, although Weissman’s inequality is stated for one-hot categorical samples, it should be viewed as a conservative worst-case reference for general simplex-valued samples.

4. Reference

  1. Weissman et al. Inequalities for the L1 deviation of the empirical distribution. Hewlett-Packard Labs, Tech 2003.
entry.summary: This post starts from the familiar problem of estimating the mean of a bounded random variable, and then follows what changes as the object of interest becomes more structured. For simplex-valued means, it is more natural to think in terms of distributional concentration, which leads to sharper and more meaningful bounds. Weissman's inequality captures this especially well in the one-hot categorical setting, while a McDiarmid-based argument extends the picture to general soft simplex-valued samples.

entry.title: Influence Functions and the Hessian Estimation

link.title: Influence Functions and the Hessian Estimation

entry.content:
1. Motivation

Understanding how sensitive a model is to its training data is both important and challenging. To assess the impact of a training point on a prediction, we often ask the following counterfactual question:

What would happen if this training point were removed, or if its value were changed slightly?

This question is central to many practical concerns in machine learning, including data quality, privacy, and security. For example, it can help us identify mislabeled or biased training examples, understand whether a model relies on sensitive or private information, and analyze how vulnerable the model is to malicious manipulation of the training data.

A straightforward way to answer such questions is to delete or perturb a training point and retrain the model. However, this is often computationally prohibitive, especially for modern large-scale models. To address this challenge, we turn to influence functions, a classical tool from robust statistics that provides a local approximation of how small changes in the training data affect the learned model. In this blog, we review influence functions for deleting and perturbing a training point, and analyze how these changes affect the model parameters, the loss, and the output. We also discuss Hessian estimation, which plays a central role in influence-function-based analysis, and explain how it can be computed efficiently in practice.

2. Setup

Consider a classification setting where the goal is to map an instance \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}\) to a label \(y \in \mathcal{Y}=[K]\). We are given training points \(\mathbf{z}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{z}_n\), where \(\mathbf{z}_i=(\mathbf{x}_i,y_i)\in \mathcal{X} imes \mathcal{Y}\). For a point \(\mathbf{z}\) and parameters \( oldsymbol{ heta}\), let \(\ell(\mathbf{z}, oldsymbol{ heta})\) be the loss, and let \( rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(\mathbf{z}_i, oldsymbol{ heta})\) be the empirical risk. The empirical minimizer is given by

\[\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \overset{ ext{def}}{=} \arg\min_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\mathbf{z}_i, oldsymbol{ heta}).\]

Assume that the empirical risk is twice-differentiable and strictly convex in \( oldsymbol{ heta}\).

3. Deleting a training point

We ask the following counterfactual question:

What would happen if this training point were removed?

3.1 Parameter change

Formally, this change is \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{-\mathbf{z}} - \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\), where

\[\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{-\mathbf{z}} \overset{ ext{def}}{=} \arg\min_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\mathbf{z}_i, oldsymbol{ heta})- rac1n\ell(\mathbf{z}, oldsymbol{ heta}).\]

Influence functions gives us an efficient approximation without retraining the model for removing \(\mathbf{z}\). The idea is to compute the parameter change if \(\mathbf{z}\) were weighted by some small \(\epsilon\), giving us new parameters

\[\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}} \overset{ ext{def}}{=} \arg\min_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\mathbf{z}_i, oldsymbol{ heta})+\epsilon\ell(\mathbf{z}, oldsymbol{ heta}).\]

Let \(\Delta_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}(\mathbf{z}) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} rac{d \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}} }{d \epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon = 0}\) be the infinitesimal parameter change. Using first-order Taylor expansion, we have

\[\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{-\mathbf{z}} - \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \approx - rac1n rac{d \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}} }{d \epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon = 0}=- rac1n \Delta_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}(\mathbf{z})\]

The infinitesimal parameter change is given by:

\[ oxed{\Delta_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}(\mathbf{z}) = - H^{-1}_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})},\]

where \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n abla^2 \ell(\mathbf{z}_i, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})\) is the Hessian and is positive definite (PD) by assumption.

Proof (Click to expand)

Recall that \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\) minimizes the empirical risk:

\[\mathcal{R}( oldsymbol{ heta}) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} rac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(\mathbf{z}_i, oldsymbol{ heta}).\]

We further assume the \(\mathcal{R}\) is twice-differentiable and strongly convex in \( oldsymbol{ heta}\), i.e.,

\[H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} \overset{ ext{def}}{=} abla^2 \mathcal{R}(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n abla_ oldsymbol{ heta}^2\ell(\mathbf{z}_i,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})\]

exists and is positive definite. This guarantees the existence of \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}^{-1}\), which we will use in the subsequent derivation.

The perturbed parameters \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}}\) can be written as

\[\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}} \overset{ ext{def}}{=} \arg\min_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\mathbf{z}_i, oldsymbol{ heta})+\epsilon\ell(\mathbf{z}, oldsymbol{ heta}).\]

Define the parameter change \(\Delta_\epsilon=\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon, \mathbf{z}} - \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\), and note that, as \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\) doesn’t depend on \(\epsilon\), the quantity we seek to compute can be written in terms of it:

\[ rac{d \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}} }{d \epsilon} = rac{d \Delta_\epsilon}{d \epsilon}\]

Since \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}}\) is a minimizer, let us examine its first-order optimality conditions:

\[\mathbf{0} = abla \mathcal{R}(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}})+\epsilon abla \ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}).\]

Next, since \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}}) ightarrow \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\) as \(\epsilon ightarrow 0\), we perform a Taylor expansion of the right-hand side:

\[\mathbf{0} \approx \left[ abla \mathcal{R}(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) + \epsilon abla L(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) ight] + \left[ abla^2 \mathcal{R}(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) + \epsilon abla^2 L(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) ight] \Delta_\epsilon,\]

Since \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\) minimize \(\mathcal{R}\), we have \( abla \mathcal{R}(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})=\mathbf{0}\). Dropping \(o(\epsilon)\) terms, we have

\[\Delta_\epsilon \approx - abla^2 \mathcal{R}(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})^{-1} abla \ell(\mathbf{z}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})\epsilon.\]

Using the definition of Hessian, we conclude that:

\[\Delta_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}(\mathbf{z}) = - H^{-1}_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}).\]
□

The parameter change due to removing \(\mathbf{z}\) can be linearly approximated as:

\[ oxed{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{-\mathbf{z}} - \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \approx rac1n H^{-1}_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})}.\]

The learned parameter \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\) can be viewed as a local equilibrium determined by all training samples. Each point contributes a gradient, which indicates the direction in which it tends to pull the model in order to reduce its own loss. Removing one sample \(\mathbf z\) removes this pull, and the optimum shifts slightly as a result.

The gradient \( abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})\) captures the individual effect of sample \(\mathbf z\), while the inverse Hessian \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}^{-1}\) adjusts this effect according to the local curvature of the loss landscape. Directions with high curvature are harder to move, whereas flatter directions are more sensitive. Therefore, this formula says that the parameter change caused by removing one point is approximately its own gradient contribution, scaled by \(1/n\) and corrected by the local geometry.

3.2 Loss change

Next, we apply the chain rule to measure how deleting \(\mathbf{z}\) changes the loss function at a test point \(\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test}\). Let

\[\Delta_{\ell}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test}) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} rac{d \ell(\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}}) }{d \epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon = 0}\]

be the infinitesimal loss change. Using first-order Taylor expansion, the loss change has the expression:

\[\ell(\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{-\mathbf{z}})-\ell(\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) \approx - rac1n \Delta_{\ell}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test}).\]

The infinitesimal loss change is given by:

\[ oxed{\Delta_{\ell}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test})= - abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})^ op H^{-1}_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})}.\]
Proof (Click to expand)
\[ egin{aligned} \Delta_{\ell}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test}) &\overset{ ext{def}}{=} rac{d \ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}})}{d\epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon=0} \ &= abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})^ op rac{d\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}}}{d\epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon=0} \ &= - abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})^ op H^{-1}_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) \end{aligned}\]
□

The loss change due to removing \(\mathbf{z}\) can be linearly approximated as:

\[ oxed{\ell(\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{-\mathbf{z}})-\ell(\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) \approx rac1n abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})^ op H^{-1}_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})}.\]

It compares the direction in which the test point would like to move the parameters with the direction contributed by the training point, after correcting for the local geometry of the loss landscape.

Let \(S(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}) := abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})^ op H^{-1}_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}).\) Then:

  • If \(S(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}) > 0\), then \(\ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{-\mathbf{z}}) - \ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) > 0,\) so removing \(\mathbf z\) increases the test loss: \(\mathbf z\) is helpful for \(\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}\).

  • If \(S(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}) < 0\), then \(\ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{-\mathbf{z}}) - \ell(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) < 0,\) so removing \(\mathbf z\) decreases the test loss: \(\mathbf z\) is harmful for \(\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}\).

  • If \(S(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}) \approx 0\), then removing \(\mathbf z\) has little first-order effect on the prediction at \(\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}\).

3.2.1 Self influence

When \(\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}=\mathbf z\), the influence reduces to the self-influence

\[\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}_{-\mathbf z}) - \ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}) \approx rac1n abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta})^ op H_{\hat{ oldsymbol heta}}^{-1} abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}).\]

Under the local convexity assumption, \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol heta}}^{-1}\) is positive definite, so this quantity is nonnegative. Thus, removing a training point typically increases its own loss. Moreover, the magnitude is not determined only by the gradient norm, but also by the local curvature: directions with smaller curvature are amplified by \(H^{-1}\), while directions with larger curvature are suppressed.

3.3 Output change

Next, we study how deleting a training point \(\mathbf{z}\) changes the model output at a test point \(\mathbf{z}_\mathsf{test}\). Let \(f(\mathbf{x}, oldsymbol{ heta})\) denote the model output. For simplicity, we first consider the scalar-output case, where \(f(\mathbf{x}, oldsymbol{ heta}) \in \mathbb{R}\). Let

\[\Delta_f(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} rac{d\,f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta}_{\epsilon,\mathbf z})}{d\epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon=0}\]

be the infinitesimal output change. Using a first-order Taylor expansion, the output change due to removing \(\mathbf z\) can be approximated as

\[f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta}_{-\mathbf z}) - f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta}) \approx - rac1n \Delta_f(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}).\]

The infinitesimal output change is given by

\[ oxed{\Delta_f(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}) = - abla_{ oldsymbol heta} f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta})^ op H_{\hat{ oldsymbol heta}}^{-1} abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta})}.\]
Proof (Click to expand)
\[ egin{aligned} \Delta_f(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}) &\overset{ ext{def}}{=} rac{d\,f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta}_{\epsilon,\mathbf z})}{d\epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon=0} \ &= abla_{ oldsymbol heta} f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta})^ op rac{d\hat{ oldsymbol heta}_{\epsilon,\mathbf z}}{d\epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon=0} \ &= - abla_{ oldsymbol heta} f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta})^ op H_{\hat{ oldsymbol heta}}^{-1} abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}). \end{aligned}\]
□

Therefore, the output change due to removing \(\mathbf z\) can be linearly approximated as

\[ oxed{ f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta}_{-\mathbf z}) - f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta}) \approx rac1n abla_{ oldsymbol heta} f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta})^ op H_{\hat{ oldsymbol heta}}^{-1} abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta})}.\]

It tells us how much the prediction at \(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}}\) changes when the contribution of training point \(\mathbf z\) is removed. The quantity \( abla_{ oldsymbol heta} f(\mathbf x_{\mathsf{test}},\hat{ oldsymbol heta})^ op H_{\hat{ oldsymbol heta}}^{-1} abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta})\) can be viewed as a curvature-adjusted alignment between the training-point gradient and the sensitivity of the test output.

3.3.1 Self influence

When \(\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}}=\mathbf z\), the formula reduces to

\[f(\mathbf x,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}_{-\mathbf z}) - f(\mathbf x,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}) \approx rac1n abla_{ oldsymbol heta} f(\mathbf x,\hat{ oldsymbol heta})^ op H_{\hat{ oldsymbol heta}}^{-1} abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}).\]

This quantity measures how much the model’s own prediction on a training point changes after that point is removed from the training set. Unlike the self-loss influence, its sign is not necessarily fixed: depending on the local geometry and on the relation between \( abla_{ oldsymbol heta} f(\mathbf x,\hat{ oldsymbol heta})\) and \( abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}),\) the output may either increase or decrease.

3.4 Special Cases

The general influence formulas apply to a broad class of differentiable models. However, in several important settings, they admit simpler and more interpretable forms.

3.4.1 Regression

In regression, the model output is typically scalar, \(f(\mathbf{x}, oldsymbol{ heta})\in \mathbb{R}\). A common choice is the squared loss

\[\ell(\mathbf{z}, oldsymbol{ heta})= rac12 \left(f(\mathbf{x}, oldsymbol{ heta})-y ight)^2\]

In this case,

\[ abla_ oldsymbol{ heta}\ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})=\left(f(\mathbf{x},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})-y ight) abla_ oldsymbol{ heta}f(\mathbf{x},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}),\]

so the influence is proportional to the prediction error \(\left(f(\mathbf{x},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})-y ight)\).

3.4.2 Classification

Consider the binary classification case, where the model produces a scalar logit \(f(\mathbf{x}, oldsymbol{ heta}) \in \mathbb{R}\). Under the cross-entropy loss,

\[\ell(\mathbf{z},{ oldsymbol{ heta}})=-y\log \sigma (f(\mathbf{x},{ oldsymbol{ heta}}))-(1-y)\log(1-\sigma (f(\mathbf{x},{ oldsymbol{ heta}})),\]

the derivative of the loss with respect to the output is

\[ rac{\partial \ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})}{\partial f}=\sigma(f(\mathbf{x}, oldsymbol{ heta}))-y.\]

Therefore, by the chain rule,

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf z,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) = igl(\sigma(f(\mathbf x,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}))-y igr) abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}f(\mathbf x,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}).\]

3.4.3 Linear models

For linear models, the influence formulas become particularly explicit because the Hessian can be written in closed form. Consider a linear predictor

\[f(\mathbf x, oldsymbol heta)= oldsymbol heta^ op \mathbf x.\]
Linear regression

For squared-loss linear regression, \(\ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol heta)= rac12( oldsymbol heta^ op\mathbf x-y)^2.\) Then

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol heta) = ( oldsymbol heta^ op\mathbf x-y)\mathbf x, \qquad abla_{ oldsymbol heta}^2\ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol heta) = \mathbf x\mathbf x^ op.\]

Hence (recall that \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} = rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2 \ell(\mathbf z_i,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})\)),

\[\hat{ oldsymbol heta}_{-\mathbf z}-\hat{ oldsymbol heta} \approx \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^ op ight)^{-1} (\hat{ oldsymbol heta}^ op\mathbf x-y)\mathbf x.\]

The loss change and the output change can be analyzed analogously.

Logistic regression

Under the binary cross-entropy loss,

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol heta}\ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol heta) = igl(\sigma( oldsymbol heta^ op\mathbf x)-y igr)\mathbf x,\]

and

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol heta}^2\ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol heta) = \sigma( oldsymbol heta^ op\mathbf x) igl(1-\sigma( oldsymbol heta^ op\mathbf x) igr)\mathbf x\mathbf x^ op.\]

Therefore,

\[\hat{ oldsymbol heta}_{-\mathbf z}-\hat{ oldsymbol heta} \approx \left( \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma(\hat{ oldsymbol heta}^ op\mathbf x_i) igl(1-\sigma(\hat{ oldsymbol heta}^ op\mathbf x_i) igr) \mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^ op ight)^{-1} igl(\sigma(\hat{ oldsymbol heta}^ op\mathbf x)-y igr)\mathbf x.\]

The loss change and the output change can be analyzed analogously.

4. Perturbing a training input

We ask the following counterfactual question:

What would happen if this training input were modified?`

For a training point \(\mathbf{z}=(\mathbf{x},y)\), define \(\mathbf{z}_{ oldsymbol{\delta}} \overset{ ext{def}}{=} (\mathbf{x}+ oldsymbol{\delta},y).\) Consider the perturbation \(\mathbf{z} ightarrow \mathbf{z}_ oldsymbol{\delta}\), and let \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\mathbf{z}_ oldsymbol{\delta},-\mathbf{z}}\) be the empirical risk minimizer on the training points with \(\mathbf{z}_ oldsymbol{\delta}\) in place of \(\mathbf{z}\). To approximate its effects, define the parameters resulting from moving \(\epsilon\) mass from \(\mathbf{z}\) onto \(\mathbf{z}_ oldsymbol{\delta}\):

\[\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon, \mathbf{z}_ oldsymbol{\delta}, -\mathbf{z}} \overset{ ext{def}}{=} \arg\min_ oldsymbol{ heta} rac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(\mathbf{z}_i, oldsymbol{ heta}) + \epsilon \ell(\mathbf{z}_ oldsymbol{\delta}, oldsymbol{ heta}) - \epsilon \ell(\mathbf{z}, oldsymbol{ heta}).\]

An analogous computation yields:

\[ rac{d\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}_{ oldsymbol\delta},-\mathbf{z}}}{d\epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon=0} = rac{d\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}_{ oldsymbol\delta}}}{d\epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon=0} - rac{d\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}}}{d\epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon=0}= - H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}^{-1} \Bigl( abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \ell(\mathbf{z}_{ oldsymbol\delta},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) - abla_{ oldsymbol{ oldsymbol heta}} \ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) \Bigr)\]

\[\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\mathbf{z}_ oldsymbol{\delta},-\mathbf{z}}=- rac1n H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}^{-1} \Bigl( abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \ell(\mathbf{z}_{ oldsymbol\delta},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) - abla_{ oldsymbol{ oldsymbol heta}} \ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) \Bigr),\]

giving us a closed-form estimate of the effect of \(\mathbf{z} ightarrow \mathbf{z}_ oldsymbol{\delta}\) on the model. Analogous equations also apply for changes in \(y\). While influence functions might appear to only work for infinitesi- mal (therefore continuous) perturbations, it is important to note that this approximation holds for arbitrary \( oldsymbol{\delta}\): the \(\epsilon\)-upweighting scheme allows us to smoothly interpolate between \(\mathbf{z}\) and \(\mathbf{z}_ oldsymbol{ heta}\). This is particularly useful for working with discrete data (e.g., in NLP) or with discrete label changes.

Assume that the input domain \(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), the parameter space \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), and the loss function \(\ell\) is differentiable with respect to both \( oldsymbol{ heta}\) and \(\mathbf{x}\). If \( oldsymbol{\delta}\) is small, then

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z}_{ oldsymbol{\delta}},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) - abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) \approx igl[ abla_{\mathbf{x}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) igr] oldsymbol{\delta},\]

\[ rac{d\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\epsilon,\mathbf{z}_{ oldsymbol{\delta}},-\mathbf{z}}}{d\epsilon} igg|_{\epsilon=0} \approx - H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}^{-1} igl[ abla_{\mathbf{x}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) igr] oldsymbol{\delta}.\]

\[ oxed{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}_{\mathbf{z}_{ oldsymbol{\delta}},-\mathbf{z}} - \hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \approx - rac1n H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}^{-1} igl[ abla_{\mathbf{x}} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf{z},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) igr] oldsymbol{\delta}}.\]

5. Hessian estimation

Except in linear models, where closed-form expressions are available, a practical bottleneck in influence functions is the computation of the Hessian \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}\), and especially its inverse. In this section, we first review the direct method (exact computation), and then discuss several efficient estimation and approximation methods, including conjugate gradients, stochastic estimation, diagonal approximation, and outer-product approximation.

5.1 Direct method

The most direct approach is to first compute the full Hessian matrix \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} = rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2 \ell(\mathbf z_i,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})\) and then compute its inverse \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}^{-1}\). However, if the model has \(p\) parameters, forming the Hessian costs \(O(np^2)\) operations and storing it requires \(O(p^2)\) memory, while matrix inversion costs an additional \(O(p^3)\). This quickly becomes prohibitive for modern models.

In PyTorch, this direct method can be implemented by defining the empirical risk as a function of the parameter vector and then calling torch.autograd.functional.hessian to obtain the full Hessian matrix. Once the Hessian is formed, one can compute its inverse explicitly. E.g.

# theta: parameter vector of shape (p,)
# loss_fn: empirical risk as a scalar function of theta
H = torch.autograd.functional.hessian(loss_fn, theta)
H_inv = torch.linalg.inv(H)

5.2 Conjugate gradient

The first technique is to avoid explict inversion of the Hessian matrix, which transforms it into an optimization problem. Since \(H_\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \succ 0\) by assumption,

\[H_\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^{-1}\mathbf{v}=\arg \min_\mathbf{t}\{ rac12\mathbf{t}^ op H_\hat{ heta}\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{v}^ op\mathbf{t}\}.\]
Proof (Click to expand)

Taking the gradient with respect to \(\mathbf t\) gives

\[ abla_{\mathbf t} \{ rac12\mathbf{t}^ op H_\hat{ heta}\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{v}^ op\mathbf{t}\} = H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}\mathbf t-\mathbf v.\]

Setting the gradient to zero, the minimizer must satisfy \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}\mathbf t=\mathbf v.\) Since \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}\) is invertible, the unique solution is

\[\mathbf t = H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}^{-1}\mathbf v.\]
□

We can solve this with conjugate gradient approaches that only require the evaluation of \(H_\hat{ oldsymbol heta} \mathbf{t}\), which takes \(O(np)\), without explicitly forming \(H_\hat{ oldsymbol heta}\). While an exact solution takes \(p\) iterations, in practice we can get a good approximation with fewer iterations

Conjugate gradient implementation (Click to expand)

Motivation: Avoiding Repeated Corrections

Let \(f(\mathbf{x})= rac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^ op A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}^ op\mathbf{x},\),where \(A\) is symmetric positive definite. To solve \(\mathbf{x}^\star=\arg\min_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{x}),\) a natural approach is gradient descent with exact line search. Define \(\mathbf{g}_k= abla f(\mathbf{x}_k)=A\mathbf{x}_k-\mathbf{b}\). The update is

\[\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k - \alpha_k \mathbf{g}_k,\]

where

\[ egin{aligned} \alpha_k &= \arg\min_\alpha f(\mathbf{x}_k - \alpha \mathbf{g}_k) \ &= \arg\min_\alpha \left[ rac{1}{2}\alpha^2 \mathbf{g}_k^ op A\mathbf{g}_k - \alpha (A\mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{b})^ op \mathbf{g}_k + \mathrm{const.} ight] \ &=\arg\min_\alpha \left[ rac{1}{2}\alpha^2 \mathbf{g}_k^ op A\mathbf{g}_k - \alpha \mathbf{g}_k^ op \mathbf{g}_k + \mathrm{const.} ight]\ &= rac{\mathbf{g}_k^ op \mathbf{g}_k}{\mathbf{g}_k^ op A \mathbf{g}_k}. \end{aligned}\]

Suppose we start from \(\mathbf{x}_0\) and perform updates along \(\mathbf{g}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{g}_{k}\), arriving at

\[\mathbf{x}_{k+1}=\mathbf{x}_0-\sum_{i=0}^{k} \alpha_i \mathbf{g}_i,\]

for some update coefficients \(\alpha_i\). Expanding the objective gives

\[ egin{aligned} f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) &= f(\mathbf{x}_0) - \sum_{i=0}^{k} \alpha_i \mathbf{g}_i^ op (A\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{b}) + rac{1}{2} \sum_{i=0}^{k} \alpha_i^2 \mathbf{g}_i^ op A \mathbf{g}_i \ &\quad+ \sum_{0 \le i < j \le k} \alpha_i \alpha_j \mathbf{g}_i^ op A\mathbf{g}_j. \end{aligned}\]

The last term captures the interactions among different search directions. Consequently, the optimal step size along one direction generally depends on the coefficients along the other directions. Thus, optimizing a new direction may change the optimal coefficient of a previously optimized direction, leading to repeated corrections.

If the directions are mutually \(A\)-conjugate, \(\mathbf{g}_i^ op A\mathbf{g}_j = 0, orall i eq j,\) all cross terms vanish. This motivates constructing mutually \(A\)-conjugate search directions instead.

From Gradient Descent to Conjugate Directions

Ideally, we want each new search direction to be \(A\)-conjugate to all previously explored directions, i.e.,

\[ oxed{ \mathbf{d}_i^ op A\mathbf{d}_j = 0, \qquad orall i eq j. }\]

In gradient descent, the update direction is always chosen as \(\mathbf{d}_k=-\mathbf{g}_k.\) To meet the \(A\)-conjugate, at timestep \(k+1\), instead of directly following \(-\mathbf{g}_{k+1}\), conjugate gradient constructs a modified search direction

\[\mathbf{d}_{k+1}=-\mathbf{g}_{k+1} + eta_k \mathbf{d}_k,\]

We first choose \( eta_k\) to make the new direction \(A\)-conjugate to the most recent direction \(\mathbf{d}_k\):

\[\mathbf{d}_{k+1}^ op A \mathbf{d}_k= 0.\]

Therefore,

\[(-\mathbf{g}_{k+1}+ eta_k\mathbf{d}_k)^ op A \mathbf{d}_k=0 \Rightarrow eta_k = rac{\mathbf{g}_{k+1}A\mathbf{d}_k}{\mathbf{d}_k^ op A \mathbf{d}_k}.\]

Again, after deriving the update direction \(\mathbf{d}_{k+1}\), we perform line search, such that

\[\mathbf{x}_{k+2} = \mathbf{x}_{k+1} + \alpha_{k+1} \mathbf{d}_{k+1}, \quad \mathrm{where} \quad \alpha_{k+1} = \arg\min_\alpha f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} + \alpha \mathbf{d}_{k+1}) =- rac{\mathbf{d}_{k+1}^ op \mathbf{g}_{k+1}}{\mathbf{d}_{k+1}^ op A\mathbf{d}_{k+1}}\]

Although this choice explicitly imposes only \(\mathbf{d}_{k+1}^ op A\mathbf{d}_k=0,\) the conjugate-gradient recurrence, together with exact line search, implies that \(\mathbf{d}_{k+1}\) is automatically \(A\)-conjugate to all earlier search directions.

Assume that the existing directions are mutually \(A\)-conjugate:

\[\mathbf{d}_i^ op A\mathbf{d}_j=0, \qquad 0\leq i<j\leq k.\]

First, we show that \(\mathbf{g}_{k+1} \perp \mathbf{d}_k= 0:\)

\[\mathbf{g}_{k+1}^ op\mathbf{d}_k=(A\mathbf{x}_{k+1}-\mathbf{b})^T\mathbf{d}_k=(\mathbf{g}_k+\alpha_k A\mathbf{d}_k)^ op \mathbf{d}_k=0.\]

Then, we show that \(\mathbf{g}_{k+1} \perp \mathbf{d}_i= 0, orall i<k:\)

\[\mathbf{g}_{k+1} = \mathbf{g}_{i+1}+\sum_{j=i+1}^{k}\alpha_jA\mathbf{d}_j,\]

we obtain

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbf{g}_{k+1}^ op\mathbf{d}_i &= (\mathbf{g}_{i+1}+\sum_{j=i+1}^{k}\alpha_jA\mathbf{d}_j)^ op \mathbf{d}_i=0. \end{aligned}\]

Therefore,

\[\mathbf{g}_{k+1}^ op\mathbf{d}_i=0, \qquad i=0,\ldots,k.\]

Moreover, since

\[\mathbf{d}_i = -\mathbf{g}_i+ eta_{i-1}\mathbf{d}_{i-1},\]

each previous gradient \(\mathbf{g}_i\) lies in the span of the previous search directions. Hence,

\[\mathbf{g}_{k+1}^ op\mathbf{g}_i=0, \qquad i=0,\ldots,k.\]

Now consider any earlier direction \(\mathbf{d}_i\) with \(i<k\). We have

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbf{d}_{k+1}^ op A\mathbf{d}_i = \left( -\mathbf{g}_{k+1} + eta_k\mathbf{d}_k ight)^ op A\mathbf{d}_i = -\mathbf{g}_{k+1}^ op A\mathbf{d}_i, \end{aligned}\]

From the gradient update at iteration \(i\),

\[\mathbf{g}_{i+1} = \mathbf{g}_i+\alpha_iA\mathbf{d}_i \Rightarrow A\mathbf{d}_i = rac{ \mathbf{g}_{i+1}-\mathbf{g}_i }{ \alpha_i }.\]

Therefore,

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbf{d}_{k+1}^ op A\mathbf{d}_i = - rac{1}{\alpha_i} \mathbf{g}_{k+1}^ op \left( \mathbf{g}_{i+1}-\mathbf{g}_i ight) = - rac{1}{\alpha_i} \left( \mathbf{g}_{k+1}^ op\mathbf{g}_{i+1} - \mathbf{g}_{k+1}^ op\mathbf{g}_i ight) =0. \end{aligned}\]

Together with the directly enforced condition

\[\mathbf{d}_{k+1}^ op A\mathbf{d}_k=0,\]

this proves that

\[\mathbf{d}_{k+1}^ op A\mathbf{d}_i=0, \qquad i=0,\ldots,k.\]

By induction, all conjugate-gradient search directions are mutually \(A\)-conjugate:

\[ oxed{ \mathbf{d}_i^ op A\mathbf{d}_j=0, \qquad orall i eq j. }\]
□

5.3 Stochastic estimation

With large datasets, standard conjugate gradient can be slow; each iteration still goes through all \(n\) training points. We use a method developed by Agarwal et al. (2017) to get an estimator that only samples a single pointper iteration, which results in significant speedups. Dropping the \(\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\) subscript for clarity, let us first introduce the approximate matrix inversion based on truncated Neumann-series. Suppose \(H\) is invertible and \(\|H\| \leq 1\) (if this is not true, we can scale the loss down without affecting the parameters), we have

\[H^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(I-H)^k.\]

Let \(H_j^{-1} \overset{ ext{def}}{=} \sum_{i=0}^j(1-H)^{i}\), the first \(j\) terms in the expansion of \(H^{-1}\). Rewrite this recursively as

\[H^{-1}_j=I + \sum_{i=1}^{j}(I-H)^{i} =I + (I-H) \sum_{i=0}^{j-1}(I-H)^{i} = I + (I-H)H_{j-1}^{-1}.\]

\(H_j^{-1} ightarrow H^{-1}\) as \(j ightarrow \infty\). The key is that at each iteration, we can substi- tute the full H with a draw from any unbiased (and faster-to-compute) estimator of \(H\) to form \( ilde{H}_j\). Since \(\mathbb{E}[ ilde{H}_j^{-1}]=H_j^{-1}\), we still have \(\mathbb{E}[ ilde{H}_j^{-1}] ightarrow H^{-1}\).

In particular, for any training point \(\mathbf z_i\), we can use \( abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2 \ell(\mathbf z_i,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})\) as an unbiased estimator of \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}.\) This leads to the following stochastic procedure: uniformly sample \(t\) points \(\mathbf z_{s_1},\ldots,\mathbf z_{s_t}\) from the training data, initialize \( ilde H_0^{-1}\mathbf v=\mathbf v,\) and recursively compute

\[ ilde H_j^{-1}\mathbf v = \mathbf v + \Bigl(I- abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2\ell(\mathbf z_{s_j},\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})\Bigr) ilde H_{j-1}^{-1}\mathbf v.\]

We then take \( ilde H_t^{-1}\mathbf v\) as the final unbiased estimate of \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}}^{-1}\mathbf v.\) In practice, we choose \(t\) large enough so that the recursion stabilizes, and to reduce variance, we repeat this procedure \(r\) times and average the results.

5.4 Outer-product approximation

Another common surrogate is to replace the Hessian by an outer-product matrix:

\[ ilde{H}= rac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{g}_i\mathbf{g}_i^ op, \quad \mathbf{g}_i = abla_ oldsymbol{ heta} \ell(\mathbf{z}_i,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}).\]

This is related to empirical Fisher or Gauss-Newton style approximations. Its appeal is that it is always positive semidefinite and often easier to estimate. However, it comes with two caveats. First, it is not the true Hessian in general. Second, it may be low-rank or severely ill-conditioned, especially in overparameterized models, so its inverse may not exist or may be numerically unstable. In practice, one usually adds damping,

\[ ilde{H}_\lambda = ilde{H} + \lambda I.\]
Why can the Hessian be approximated by an outer-product matrix? (Click to expand)

Replacing the Hessian by an outer-product matrix is particularly natural for nonlinear least-squares problems. Assume the loss can be written as

\[\ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol{ heta}) = rac{1}{2n} \sum_{i=1}^m e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta})^2,\]

where \(\mathbf e(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) = igl(e_1(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}),\ldots,e_m(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) igr)^ op \in\mathbb R^m\)

is the vector of residuals. Let

\[\mathbf g(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\mathbf e(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) = egin{bmatrix} abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} e_1(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) & \cdots & abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} e_m(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb R^{p imes m}\]

be its Jacobian matrix. By the chain rule, the gradient of the loss is

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol{ heta}) = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^m e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) = rac{1}{n}\mathbf g(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta})\,\mathbf e(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}).\]

Differentiating once more gives the Hessian

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2 \ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol{ heta}) = rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^m abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta})^ op + rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^m e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2 e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}).\]

Equivalently, in matrix form,

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2 \ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol{ heta}) = rac{1}{n}\mathbf g(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta})\mathbf g(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta})^ op + rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^m e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}) abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2 e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta}).\]

When the residual terms \(e_i(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta})\) are small, the second term is negligible. In that case, we obtain the approximation

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2 \ell(\mathbf z, oldsymbol{ heta}) \approx rac{1}{n}\mathbf g(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta})\mathbf g(\mathbf x, oldsymbol{ heta})^ op.\]

This motivates the outer-product approximation to the Hessian. In practice, one may then replace the empirical-risk Hessian \(H_{\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}} = rac1n\sum_{j=1}^n abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^2 \ell(\mathbf z_j,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})\) by \( ilde H = rac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \mathbf g(\mathbf x_j,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}) \mathbf g(\mathbf x_j,\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})^ op.\)

□

5.5 Diagonal approximation

Previous methods (direct method, conjugate gradient and stochastic estimation) produce unbiased estimation of Hessian (or related computation). A much cheaper approximation is to retain only the diagonal of the Hessian or inverse Hessian:

\[H_\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}^{-1}\approx ext{diag}(H_\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}})^{-1}.\]

This ignores cross-parameter interactions, so it is clearly less faithful than the full matrix. However, it is simple, memory-efficient, and often good enough when one only needs a rough ranking of influential points. In practice, we can further simplify the computation by restricting the estimation it to the last layer, reducing complexity from quadratic to essentially linear in the number of parameters.

5.6 Validation

Here, we empirically compare the above-mentioned Hessian estimation methods on 10-class MNIST using a logistic regression model. We train the model with L-BFGS and \(L_2\) regularization of 0.01, with \(n=55{,}000\) training samples and \(p=7{,}840\) parameters. We arbitrarily select a misclassified test point \(\mathbf{z}_{\mathsf{test}}\). Among all training points, we take the 500 points \(\mathbf z\) with the largest values of \(\Delta_\ell(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}})\), and for each of them we compare the estimated value of \(- rac1n\Delta_\ell(\mathbf z,\mathbf z_{\mathsf{test}})\) under the different estimation methods, with the true change in test loss obtained by removing that point and retraining the model.

The direct method and conjugate gradient (CG) align almost perfectly with the actual leave-one-out retraining results, showing that influence functions can be highly accurate when the Hessian inverse is computed reliably. Stochastic estimation and outer-product approximation still capture the overall trend, but with noticeably larger variance. In contrast, the diagonal approximation performs substantially worse, indicating that the off-diagonal structure of the Hessian is important even in this simple logistic-regression setting. Overall, the experiments reveal a clear trade-off between efficiency and accuracy: direct inversion and CG are the most accurate, stochastic and outer-product methods are reasonable approximations, and the diagonal approximation is too crude for precise prediction.

Reference

  1. Pang Wei Koh and Percy Liang. Understanding black-box predictions via influence functions. In ICML 2017.
  2. Nickl et al. The memory perturbation equation: understanding model’s sensitivity to data. In NeurIPS 2023.
  3. Agarwal et al. Second order stochastic optimization in linear time. JMLR 2017.
entry.summary: This blog reviews influence functions as a practical tool for understanding how individual training points affect a model’s parameters, loss, and predictions. Starting from empirical risk minimization, it derives first-order approximations for deleting or perturbing a training sample, and discusses several ways to estimate the inverse Hessian in practice, including direct inversion, conjugate gradients, stochastic estimation, diagonal approximation, and outer-product approximation.
